Why A for Signal

Signal's description promises "a dark opening" and names events; A is the only one where the photos carry that energy. The overlay tiles put each project's name on its photo, so the grid scans as a portfolio of named projects rather than anonymous pictures, and one clear All projects link avoids four identical links in a row (screen-reader users often hear links out of context, WCAG 2.4.4). B is calmer but reads close to Harbour with a different font, which undercuts having three distinct templates.

Accessibility: the opening veil is the dark style at Medium (65%); Crust raises it automatically if white text would drop under 4.5:1. Overlay tiles use the dark style with a strong tint for the same reason. Every photo has a real description, and every link says where it goes.

  • Feel: more atmospheric, closer to Harbour's structure.

Why A for Corner

Local-shop visitors come with a task: what do you sell, when are you open, where are you. A answers "what" in the first scroll with named products and prices (recognition over recall: the visitor sees the loaf, not a category), and the split opening keeps the butter-yellow brand colour visible instead of buried under a photo. B is prettier at first glance but the shop front is busy, needs a heavy pale wash to keep navy text readable, and its untitled gallery tells visitors less.

Accessibility: in A no text sits on a photo except the tool-wall band, which uses the pale style at Strong (82%) so navy text stays above 4.5:1. Card titles are real headings (h3) under the section's h2, so heading order holds. Product cards stay readable when photos are off.
